content: 1. Conduct studies to assess the burden of disease for six causes of meningitis. 2. Carry out surveys among policymakers to determine the timing of vaccine introduction and assess the capacity for resource mobilization. 3. Integrate laboratory support for measles and polio, provide training, and ensure supplies for active surveillance of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP), measles, and maternal and neonatal tetanus (MNT) in all districts. 4. Validate and improve the quality of immunization coverage data. 5. Implement coverage surveys every three years to monitor progress. 6. Establish hospital-based surveillance systems for rotavirus, meningitis, and pneumonia. 7. Conduct serological surveys to assess immunity levels in the population. 8. Increase demand for immunizations, aiming for DTP3 coverage above 90% and a dropout rate between DTP1 and DTP3 of less than 5%. 9. Conduct knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) studies, and incorporate lessons learned into policy and practice. 10. Include maternal and neonatal tetanus (MNT) in key messages for strengthening routine immunization. 11. Develop communication plans that emphasize improving outreach and include key messages for routine immunization strengthening. 12. Engage the National Immunization Technical Advisory Group (NITAG), professional associations, and the Interagency Coordinating Committee (ICC) in regular updates on adverse events following immunization (AEFI). 13. Hold quarterly press conferences to discuss immunization issues and disseminate press releases on selected topics. 14. Community financing refers to various mechanisms for funding health services, such as micro-insurance, community health funds, and revolving drug funds. 15. Cost-benefit analysis evaluates and compares all costs and benefits of different health interventions, such as malaria control versus immunization, to determine which provides the most benefits per unit cost. 16. Cost-effectiveness analysis compares different methods of achieving the same objective to identify the least expensive way to achieve it, often measured by outcomes like lives saved or children vaccinated. 17. Costing involves determining the total cost of a program over a specific period, such as one year. 18. Cost per capita links total immunization costs to the country’s population to assess the affordability of the program. 19. Cost per dose calculates the total immunization cost relative to the number of vaccine doses administered. 20. Cost per DTP3 child estimates the resources required to immunize a child with three doses of DTP3, based on the number of children under one year of age who received their third dose. 21. Debt relief involves refinancing or canceling the principal and/or interest payments on loans to developing countries. 22. Effectiveness measures the extent to which a program achieves its objectives, such as a polio program eliminating polio. 23. Expenditure refers to the amount of money spent on goods or services during a specific period. 24. A financial plan is a document resulting from financial planning, outlining resource allocation and sustainability strategies. 25. Financial sustainability refers to a country’s ability to mobilize and efficiently use domestic and external resources to achieve immunization targets reliably. 26. A financial sustainability plan (FSP) is a structured approach to addressing financing challenges and supporting mediumand long-term program objectives. 27. Financing refers to the amount and sources of money available for a program or activity. 28. A financing gap is the difference between the funding needed to achieve program objectives and the available financing from government and partners. 29. GAVI is a public-private partnership that includes governments, UNICEF, WHO, the vaccine industry, and other partners, focusing on increasing vaccine access and strengthening immunization programs in developing countries. 30. A health sector strategic plan (HSSP) outlines goals, objectives, and priorities for delivering health services, serving as a framework for detailed planning. 31. Highly Indebted Poor Countries II (HIPC II) is a World Bank-managed program offering accelerated debt relief to eligible countries meeting specific criteria. 32. An Interagency Coordinating Committee (ICC) is a group of immunization partners involved in funding and providing immunization services in a country. 33. Indicators are measures used to assess program performance, often monitored at regular intervals and compared to a baseline or standard. 34. A medium-term expenditure framework (MTEF) links policy, planning, and budgeting over a medium-term period, typically three years. 35. The Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) are eight United Nations goals aimed at eradicating poverty, improving health, and promoting global development. 36. Multilateral agencies, such as WHO or the African Development Bank, are organizations governed by multiple countries and act independently to fulfill their mandates. 37. A poverty reduction strategy paper (PRSP) outlines a country’s policies and programs to promote growth, reduce poverty, and identify external financing needs. 38. Recurrent costs are annual expenses required to maintain a program, such as salaries, vaccines, fuel, equipment maintenance, and disease surveillance. 39. A sector-wide approach (SWAp) pools donor support and funding to align with a comprehensive vision for the health sector. 40. Shared costs refer to resources used across multiple health services, such as facilities and staff providing both immunization and other health services. 41. Social mobilization involves advocacy and community education to raise awareness and encourage immunization uptake. 42. Supplementary immunization activities (SIAs) are additional immunization efforts, such as campaigns to eliminate polio, conducted alongside routine programs. 43. UNICEF is a United Nations agency focusing on children’s rights, with childhood immunization as one of its priorities. 44. User fees are charges for goods or services, such as fees for curative services, but are not recommended for immunization programs. 45. WHO is the United Nations agency for health, providing global leadership and technical support. 46. Acceptability measures how well a service meets community standards and cultural needs, often assessed through KAP studies. 47. Accessibility evaluates how easily clients can use services, with first immunization contact coverage often serving as an indicator. 48. An audit examines the appropriateness of an organization’s operations, including financial, technical, or data quality audits. 49. Accountability requires managers to demonstrate compliance with plans, budgets, and standards, and to report performance results accurately. 50. A baseline provides data describing the initial situation addressed by a program, serving as a starting point for measuring progress. 51. A benchmark is a reference point or standard used to assess performance or achievement, often as an intermediate target. 52. Civil society organizations (CSOs) are non-governmental, non-profit entities that provide public services. 53. Criteria are standards used to evaluate whether a program meets expectations and to set priorities based on strategic values, efficiency, equity, impact, and feasibility. 54. Data sources refer to the origins of collected information, such as records, individuals, or documents. 55. Efficacy measures the beneficial results of an intervention under ideal conditions. 56. Efficiency assesses how well inputs (e.g., funds, expertise, time) are used to achieve outputs. 57. Equity refers to fairness in service provision, ensuring equal treatment for those with the same needs and proportional treatment for those with different needs. 58. Evaluation systematically determines the relevance, effectiveness, and impact of a program or policy in achieving its objectives. 59. External evaluation is conducted by entities outside the program being evaluated, ensuring independence from those responsible for program design and implementation. 60. Feedback involves transmitting findings, conclusions, and recommendations from monitoring and evaluation to facilitate learning and decision-making. 61. Formative evaluation, conducted during project implementation, aims to improve performance and may address compliance or legal requirements. 62. Frameworks for planning provide reference points for setting priorities and organizing strategies, such as national health sector plans or immunization system components. 63. A goal represents the higher-order aim of a program, such as preventing mortality, morbidity, or disability in immunization contexts. 64. Health system building blocks include service delivery, workforce, health information, medical technologies, financing, and governance, which interact to form a complete system. 65. Human resource management ensures adequate staffing in terms of numbers, distribution, quality, and motivation to achieve organizational objectives. 66. Immunization system components include program management, human resources, financing, vaccines and logistics, service delivery, surveillance, demand generation, and communication. 67. Impact refers to the overall effect of achieving specific results, including planned or unplanned, positive or negative, direct or indirect changes. 68. Inputs are resources such as personnel, finances, and equipment necessary to produce outputs and achieve objectives. 69. Internal evaluation is managed or conducted by entities within the program being evaluated. 70. Leadership and governance involve strategic policy frameworks, oversight, coalition building, accountability, regulations, and system design.
